title: Foreign-policy values cross-cut U.S. political coalitions
source_unit: Pew Research Center 2026 Political Typology survey of the American Trends Panel

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the American Trends Panel

superpower_importance_national.unit: percent saying sole military superpower status is at least somewhat important

allies_compromise_national.unit: percent saying the U.S. should consider allies' interests even when compromise is required

leftward_progressives_superpower.unit: percent saying sole-superpower status is at least somewhat important

leftward_progressives_allies.unit: group position favoring consideration of allies' interests even with compromise

no_apologies_right_own_interests.unit: group position favoring following U.S. interests when allies disagree

nato_group_split.value: most groups favorable; seven-in-ten or more unfavorable in No Apologies Right and Faith First Conservatives

observations.method: Descriptive comparison of foreign-policy questions across nine cluster-derived political typology groups; the typology uses 30 value and attitude questions.
observations.uncertainty: The survey measures stated judgments at one field period. Cluster boundaries, question wording, partisan composition, and current events can shape the group contrasts; the source does not identify causal mechanisms or durable identities.
observations.subgroup: Nine Pew political typology groups, including groups that are internally cross-pressured and groups with different partisan orientations.
observations.counterinterpretation: Support for military primacy can coexist with support for alliances, and opposition to primacy can coexist with strong alliance support. A stated preference does not establish defense spending, burden sharing, willingness to fight, government policy, alliance durability, or foreign reaction.

related_sources.claim: The companion report documents the survey design, nine-group typology, and detailed tables.

boundary: This record adds a cross-pressure map of U.S. foreign-policy values within domestic political coalitions. It does not follow respondents into voting, protest, defense spending, military service, alliance burden sharing, government decisions, partner consent, or external geopolitical behavior.
